questions.stem: What is the original source of almost all the energy that flows through an ecosystem?
options: Heat from the soil
Nutrients from decomposers
Minerals dissolved in water
Light from the sun
questions.explanation: Producers capture light energy in photosynthesis and store it as chemical energy in organic compounds, which then passes to consumers. Nutrients and minerals are matter that cycles; they are not sources of energy.

questions.stem: Why is energy said to flow through an ecosystem while matter cycles?
options: Energy is lost as heat at each trophic level and must be resupplied, but atoms are reused
Energy is recycled by decomposers back to producers, while atoms are lost to the atmosphere
Energy and matter both cycle, but energy moves faster because it is lighter than matter
Energy is created by producers in photosynthesis, while matter is used up by consumers
questions.explanation: Each transfer loses energy as heat from respiration, which cannot be reused by producers, so the sun must keep supplying it. Atoms of carbon, nitrogen and other elements are passed around and reused, so matter cycles; decomposers recycle matter, not energy.

questions.stem: Primary consumers in a grassland take in 1500 kJ per square metre per year and secondary consumers take in 120 kJ per square metre per year. What is the efficiency of energy transfer between these levels?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = 120 / 1500 x 100 = 8%. Dividing the wrong way gives 12.5 (as a ratio, not a percentage), and forgetting to multiply by 100 gives 0.08.

questions.stem: Which is the main reason that only a small fraction of the energy in one trophic level reaches the next?
options: Most is stored permanently in the bodies of organisms, so it can never pass to another level
Most is reflected by the bodies of consumers, so it never enters the next trophic level
Most is returned to the producers by decomposers, so it bypasses the higher trophic levels
Most is lost as heat from respiration or stays in parts not eaten or digested
questions.explanation: Organisms use most of the energy they take in for respiration, which releases heat, and much of the rest is in bones, wood or faeces that the next level does not assimilate. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five levels.

questions.stem: In a food web, a snake eats frogs and mice; frogs eat insects; mice eat seeds and insects; insects eat leaves. Which organism feeds at more than one trophic level?
options: The insect
The leaf
The snake
The frog
questions.explanation: The snake is a third-order consumer when it eats a frog (leaves, insect, frog, snake) and a second- or third-order consumer when it eats a mouse, depending on whether the mouse ate seeds or insects. The frog only eats insects, so it is always a second-order consumer.

questions.stem: In the food web where a snake eats frogs and mice, frogs eat insects, mice eat seeds and insects, and insects eat leaves, a disease kills most of the frogs. What is the most likely short-term effect?
options: Insects increase, and the snake eats more mice, so mouse numbers fall
Insects decrease, because frogs are the only organism that eats them
Mice increase, because snakes stop feeding until frogs have recovered
Leaves increase, because frogs eat leaves as well as eating insects
questions.explanation: With fewer frogs, fewer insects are eaten, so insects increase, and the snake switches to its other prey, the mouse. Mice also eat insects, so insects do not decrease, and frogs do not eat leaves.

questions.stem: What does a pyramid of biomass show?
options: The number of species found at each trophic level
The dry mass of organisms at each trophic level at one time
The number of individual organisms at each trophic level
The energy passed between trophic levels over one year
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid represents the mass of organisms at each trophic level, usually as dry mass per unit area. A pyramid of numbers counts individuals, and a pyramid of energy shows energy flow over time.

questions.stem: In some oceans, the biomass of zooplankton at a given time is greater than the biomass of the phytoplankton they eat. How is this possible?
options: Biomass pyramids are always inverted in water because organisms there weigh less
Phytoplankton reproduce so quickly that a small standing biomass can feed a larger one
Zooplankton make their own food by photosynthesis, so they do not rely on phytoplankton
Energy increases at each trophic level in the ocean, unlike in ecosystems on land
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid is a snapshot. Phytoplankton are eaten fast but replaced very fast, so their small standing mass supports a larger mass of longer-lived zooplankton. Energy pyramids are never inverted, because energy is always lost between levels.

questions.stem: A single large gum tree supports thousands of insects, which are eaten by a few birds. How would a pyramid of numbers and a pyramid of biomass for this chain compare?
options: The numbers pyramid is broad at the base, but the biomass pyramid is narrow at the base
The numbers pyramid is narrow at the base, but the biomass pyramid is broad at the base
Both pyramids are narrow at the base, because there is only one producer in the chain
Both pyramids are broad at the base, because producers always outnumber consumers
questions.explanation: One tree is one individual, so the numbers pyramid has a tiny base under thousands of insects. The tree's mass far exceeds that of the insects, so the biomass pyramid still has a broad base.

questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
options: Cellular respiration
Decomposition
Combustion
Photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis fixes carbon dioxide into organic compounds. Respiration, decomposition (which is respiration by decomposers) and combustion all release carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Which part of the carbon cycle stores carbon for millions of years?
options: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the air of the soil
The bodies of consumers such as large mammals
Fossil fuels and carbonate rocks such as limestone
The leaves of deciduous trees and grasses
questions.explanation: Organic matter buried without decay forms coal, oil and gas, and marine shells form limestone; both hold carbon for geological time. Leaves, soil air and animal bodies return their carbon within years to decades.

questions.stem: In the nitrogen cycle, what is nitrogen fixation?
options: The release of ammonia from dead organisms and wastes by decomposers
The uptake of nitrate ions from the soil by the roots of green plants
The conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia or other usable compounds
The conversion of nitrate in the soil back into nitrogen gas by soil bacteria
questions.explanation: Most organisms cannot use the nitrogen gas in air. Fixation, by bacteria such as Rhizobium in legume root nodules, by lightning or by industry, turns it into usable compounds. Converting nitrate to nitrogen gas is denitrification.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows nitrification in the soil?
options: Proteins, then amino acids, then ammonium ions
Ammonium ions, then nitrite ions, then nitrate ions
Nitrate ions, then nitrite ions, then nitrogen gas
Nitrogen gas, then ammonium ions, then proteins
questions.explanation: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite and then nitrite to nitrate, which plants absorb. Nitrate to nitrogen gas is denitrification, and proteins to ammonium is ammonification by decomposers.

questions.stem: A paddock is waterlogged for weeks, leaving the soil short of oxygen. Which change to the nitrogen cycle is most likely, and why?
options: More nitrogen fixation, because legumes grow fastest in flooded soil
Less ammonification, because decomposers only work in dry conditions
More denitrification, because the bacteria involved thrive without oxygen
More nitrification, because nitrifying bacteria need waterlogged conditions
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in place of oxygen when oxygen is scarce, so waterlogging converts soil nitrate to nitrogen gas and reduces fertility. Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so nitrification slows.

questions.stem: What role do decomposers such as fungi and bacteria play in nutrient cycling?
options: They convert nitrogen gas directly into proteins that animals can then digest
They store nutrients permanently, removing them from circulation in the ecosystem
They break down dead matter and wastes, releasing nutrients for producers
They capture light energy and convert it into chemical energy in organic compounds
questions.explanation: Decomposers return carbon to the air as carbon dioxide and release mineral nutrients such as ammonium into the soil. Without them, nutrients would stay locked in dead material and producers would run short.

questions.stem: How do plants contribute to the water cycle?
options: They prevent evaporation by storing all rainfall in their tissues
They convert water vapour in the air into liquid water in their roots
They take up soil water and release water vapour by transpiration
They produce water by photosynthesis and release it into the soil
questions.explanation: Roots absorb soil water, and most of it evaporates from leaves through stomata as transpiration, returning water vapour to the air. Photosynthesis uses water rather than producing it overall.

questions.stem: What is an organism's ecological niche?
options: The physical location where it lives, such as a hollow log or a rock pool
The total number of organisms of its species living in a given area
The highest trophic level that its species can reach in a food web
Its role, including its food, habitat, activity and tolerance ranges
questions.explanation: A niche is the full set of conditions and resources a species uses and its role in the community. The physical place alone is its habitat.

questions.stem: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in nodules on the roots of wattles. What does this tell you about microorganisms in ecosystems?
options: They all compete with plants, taking nutrients that plants would otherwise use
They fill specific niches, and some supply nutrients to plants
They have no niche of their own, because they are too small to use resources
They are all decomposers, so their only role is breaking down dead matter
questions.explanation: Microorganisms occupy many distinct niches: decomposers, nitrogen fixers, nitrifiers, pathogens and partners in mutualisms. Root nodule bacteria supply fixed nitrogen to the plant in return for sugars.

questions.stem: Two introduced fish species with the same diet and spawning sites are released into a dam. Ten years later only one remains. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Succession: one species always replaces another as a habitat matures
Keystone species: the surviving species controls the whole community
Competitive exclusion: two species cannot share the same niche for long
Carrying capacity: the dam can only support one species of any kind
questions.explanation: When two species compete for exactly the same resources, the better competitor eventually excludes the other. Succession is a sequence of changing communities, not the result of two species sharing one niche.

questions.stem: Ecologists describe some species as keystone species. What does this term mean?
options: A species with an effect on community structure far beyond its abundance
The species with the greatest total biomass in an ecosystem at any given time
The first species to colonise bare rock at the start of primary succession
A species that is found only in one particular region and nowhere else on Earth
questions.explanation: Removing a keystone species changes the community much more than its numbers or biomass would predict. The species with the most biomass is a dominant species, and the first colonist is a pioneer species.

questions.stem: Along the North American Pacific coast, sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze kelp. Where otters were hunted out, urchins multiplied and kelp forests became bare 'urchin barrens'. What does this show?
options: Sea urchins are producers, so their increase reduced the kelp's food supply
Kelp is a keystone species, since it was the organism most affected
Sea otters compete with kelp for space, so their loss allowed urchins to grow
Sea otters are a keystone species whose loss changed the whole community
questions.explanation: Though not abundant, otters keep urchins in check, which protects the kelp and all the species that depend on it. Kelp was most affected, but a keystone species is defined by the effect of its loss, not by being affected.

questions.stem: Why might the loss of a keystone predator be more damaging to an ecosystem than the loss of a common prey species with greater biomass?
options: Prey species are never eaten by more than one predator, so they are easily replaced
The predator is a producer at the base of the food web and supplies all the energy
The predator controls populations that would otherwise reshape the community
Predators always have more biomass than prey, so their loss removes more energy
questions.explanation: A keystone predator can hold down a consumer that would otherwise strip out producers or competitors. Its influence comes from its interactions, not its biomass; predators usually have less biomass than their prey.

questions.stem: A drought lasting several years reduces the grass in a reserve. How is the carrying capacity for grazing wallabies affected?
options: It falls only if the wallaby population was already above the old limit
It falls, because the food supply limiting the population has shrunk
It rises, because fewer wallabies compete for each remaining grass plant
It stays the same, because carrying capacity is fixed for each species
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity depends on resources, so a climatic event that reduces food lowers it. It is not fixed; it changes as abiotic and biotic factors change.

questions.stem: How does primary succession differ from secondary succession?
options: Primary ends in a climax community; secondary never reaches a stable community
Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains after a disturbance
Primary is caused by humans; secondary is caused by natural events such as fire and flood
Primary involves only plants; secondary involves only the animals that return afterwards
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts on bare surfaces such as new lava or exposed rock with no soil. Secondary succession follows a disturbance like fire or clearing that leaves soil and often seeds, so it is usually faster.

questions.stem: Why are lichens often the pioneer species on bare rock?
options: They are the tallest plants, so they shade out any species that arrives later
They are consumers, so they feed on the animals that first arrive on the rock
They tolerate harsh conditions and help break down rock, beginning soil formation
They need deep, fertile soil, so they grow first wherever soil is already present
questions.explanation: Lichens can survive on bare rock with few nutrients and little water. Acids they release and their trapping of dust and organic matter start to build a thin soil that other species can colonise.

questions.stem: During succession, early colonising plants add organic matter and shade to the soil, and later species that need richer, cooler soil then replace them. What does this illustrate?
options: Each new species reduces the soil quality, so only tolerant species can follow
Species change the abiotic conditions, which in turn changes which species can establish
Abiotic conditions are fixed, so the later species must have arrived first but been hidden
Later species always outcompete earlier ones because they are larger in every habitat
questions.explanation: Succession is driven by feedback: organisms alter the soil, light and moisture, and the altered conditions favour different species. This continues until a relatively stable community forms.

questions.stem: Students compare quadrats in old fields abandoned 2, 10, 30 and 60 years ago, assuming each represents a stage of one sequence. What is the main weakness of this approach?
options: Succession is too fast to see differences between fields of different ages
Older fields always contain fewer species, so the comparison adds nothing
The fields may differ in soil, history and seed sources, not just in age
Quadrats cannot be used to measure plant communities in fields of any age
questions.explanation: Substituting space for time assumes each site followed the same path, but sites may differ in soil, past use or nearby seed sources. Repeated surveys of one site over time avoid this, though they take much longer.

questions.stem: Thick coal seams are found in places that are now dry and treeless. What does this evidence suggest about the past ecosystem?
options: The area once had swampy forests where plant matter was buried undecayed
The area was once a deep ocean where marine animals were buried in sediment
The area was once a desert where wind deposited sand over the plant remains
The area has always been dry, because coal forms only under dry conditions
questions.explanation: Coal forms from large amounts of plant material buried in waterlogged, low-oxygen conditions such as swamps, where decay is slow. Its presence shows that the area once supported abundant vegetation.

questions.stem: Fossil marine shells are found in limestone high on an inland plateau. What can be concluded?
options: The shells were carried inland by birds and then turned into limestone on land
Marine animals once lived on the plateau surface in freshwater lakes and rivers
Limestone forms only on mountains, so the shells must have been moved there later
The rock formed in a marine environment and was later uplifted or the sea retreated
questions.explanation: Limestone with marine fossils forms on the sea floor, so the area was once under the sea. Earth movements or falling sea levels have since left the rock far above the present coast.

questions.stem: A lake sediment core shows mostly eucalypt pollen in its lower layers, then a layer rich in charcoal, then mostly grass pollen in its upper layers. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: Grassland that gradually changed into eucalypt forest after a fire
Eucalypt forest that has remained unchanged since the core began forming
Flooding that killed the grasses and allowed eucalypts to take over
Fire followed by a shift from eucalypt-dominated vegetation to grassland
questions.explanation: Lower layers are older, so the sequence runs from eucalypt pollen, to charcoal recording fire, to grass pollen. Reading the core from top to bottom as if the top were oldest gives the reverse sequence.

questions.stem: Why is the fossil record useful evidence of past ecosystems?
options: It shows only species that are still living today, so change can be measured
It forms only from soft-bodied organisms, which tell us most about past climate
It records organisms from different times and shows how communities changed
It preserves every organism that ever lived, so past ecosystems are fully known
questions.explanation: Fossils in rock layers of different ages show which organisms lived together and how this changed. The record is incomplete, because hard parts preserve far better and most organisms never fossilise.

questions.stem: Which human activity reduces biodiversity mainly through habitat destruction?
options: Clearing native woodland for housing
Overfishing a single species of fish
Releasing excess fertiliser into rivers
Hunting a large bird species for food
questions.explanation: Land clearing removes the habitat that many species need. Overfishing and hunting are over-exploitation of particular species, and fertiliser run-off is pollution.

questions.stem: Why does replacing a native grassland with a wheat monoculture reduce biodiversity?
options: Wheat uses no water, so the soil dries out and all organisms leave
One crop replaces many plants and supports far fewer animal species
Wheat produces chemicals that kill every animal that tries to feed on it
Monocultures increase the number of plant species by adding a new crop
questions.explanation: A monoculture provides a single food and habitat type, so the many species that depended on the native plants decline. It also tends to favour a few pest species that specialise on the crop.

questions.stem: Climate has changed naturally in the past over thousands of years. Why are current human impacts of particular concern for ecosystems?
options: They affect only abiotic factors, so living species are not affected by the changes
They are smaller in magnitude than natural change, but they last for a longer time
They cause change so fast that many species cannot adapt, move or recover
They are the only cause of ecosystem change, so ecosystems never changed before humans
questions.explanation: The course stresses the magnitude, duration and speed of change. Human activities can drive large changes within decades, too fast for many populations to adapt or shift their range; ecosystems did change before humans, but usually more slowly.

questions.stem: A food web model built from a survey is used to predict what would happen if a predator were removed. What determines how reliable the prediction is?
options: Whether the model was drawn before or after the fieldwork
How representative the survey sample was of the whole ecosystem
How many colours were used to draw the food web diagram
Whether the predator is the largest species in the ecosystem
questions.explanation: Models are extrapolated from sample data, so they are only as reliable as the sampling. A small or biased sample may miss feeding links, making predictions wrong.

questions.stem: A survey of a forest's food web is carried out only on summer days. Which limitation is the most important when using this model to predict year-round effects?
options: Seasonal and nocturnal species and their feeding links may be missing
Summer data cannot show producers, because plants stop growing in summer
Daytime surveys always record too many predators compared with prey
The model will be too complex, because summer has the most species
questions.explanation: Sampling at one season and time of day may miss migratory, seasonal or nocturnal species and the links between them. The model would then be unrepresentative and its predictions less reliable.

questions.stem: Why do ecologists use models such as food webs and successional models?
options: To show every interaction exactly, since models leave nothing out
To prove that an ecosystem will never change from its current state
To simplify complex interactions and predict the effects of change
To replace fieldwork, since models are always more accurate than data
questions.explanation: Models simplify real systems so that patterns can be understood and changes predicted. They always leave things out, so they must be tested against new data and refined.
